title: Shadow IT to Customer Data at Northwind
subtitle: A fictional external-to-internal breach for training
disclaimer: Fictional training scenario. Northwind Logistics is an invented company; all hosts, buckets, and timestamps are made up. It exists to show how an ordinary attack-surface gap — one forgotten subdomain — can chain all the way to customer data.
summary: Northwind Logistics thought its attack surface was small. It wasn't. This fictional replay follows an attacker who starts with nothing but the company name, finds a **forgotten staging subdomain** in certificate-transparency logs, and chains a debug endpoint → a world-readable cloud backup → a leaked CI deploy key → a flat internal network, ending at the customer database. Every link is a routine ASM finding. Press play to watch a small oversight become a breach.

stages.name: External discovery & initial access
stages.note: passive recon into a forgotten host

events.title: Certificate-transparency sweep
events.detail: Starting from just the company name, the attacker queries certificate-transparency logs and passive DNS for anything ending in northwind.example — no packet ever touches Northwind.

events.title: A forgotten staging host
events.detail: One certificate stands out: staging-payments.northwind.example, issued months ago and never decommissioned. httpx confirms it is live and serving a debug build.

events.title: Debug endpoint exposed
events.detail: The staging build left a debug endpoint enabled that echoes environment variables — including a set of cloud credentials that were never supposed to leave CI.

events.title: World-readable backup bucket
events.detail: The leaked credentials list an S3 bucket of nightly backups — and its bucket policy is world-readable. The attacker downloads a database backup and a CI configuration archive.

events.title: Deploy key in the backup
events.detail: Inside the CI archive is a long-lived deploy key. It grants access to the CI runner — a machine that, unlike the perimeter, lives inside the corporate VPC.

events.title: A foothold inside the VPC
events.detail: The CI runner sits on a flat internal network with no segmentation between build infrastructure and production services. From here everything internal is reachable.

events.title: Flat network to the database
events.detail: The customer database accepts connections from anything in the VPC. The same credentials from the debug endpoint work here too — they were reused.

events.title: Customer PII exfiltration
events.detail: The attacker dumps the customer table and exfiltrates it. Elapsed time from 'just the company name' to customer data: under five hours.
commands: pg_dump -h db.northwind.internal -U svc_payments -t customers customers > out.sql

lessons: Attack surface is what you forgot, not what you remember. staging-payments was a real host with a real certificate that nobody was watching — certificate-transparency monitoring would have flagged it the day it was issued.
Debug endpoints that echo environment variables are credential leaks waiting to happen. Ship builds with debug disabled, and never put production credentials in a staging environment.
A public storage bucket turns one leaked key into a data breach. Enforce block-public-access at the account level and treat every backup as if it contains the crown jewels — because it does.
Long-lived deploy keys in backups chain cloud access into network access. Use short-lived, scoped credentials, and keep secrets out of anything that gets backed up in the clear.
A flat network means one foothold equals full reach. Segment build infrastructure from production, and don't let a CI runner talk to the customer database.
Every link here was a routine ASM finding — a forgotten subdomain, an open bucket, a reused credential. Continuous discovery catches these while they are still just findings, not incident timelines.

controls.label: Monitor certificate transparency; decommission stale hosts
controls.detail: Watch CT logs for every certificate issued under your domain and retire hosts you no longer run. The forgotten staging subdomain never becomes a live target — the single highest-leverage control, because it's the one that knows your attack surface.

controls.label: Disable debug endpoints; no prod credentials in staging
controls.detail: Ship builds with debug disabled and never place production cloud credentials in a staging environment. The debug endpoint has nothing to leak, so the foothold on staging never becomes cloud access.

controls.label: Short-lived scoped credentials; no secrets in backups
controls.detail: Keep long-lived deploy keys out of anything that gets backed up in the clear, and scope credentials tightly. Reading the backup bucket yields no reusable key, so the CI runner stays out of reach.

controls.label: Isolate CI runners from the production network
controls.detail: Put build infrastructure on its own segment with no path to production services. A foothold on the CI runner reaches nothing internal.

controls.label: Segment and restrict the customer database
controls.detail: Don't let anything in the VPC reach the customer database; require specific, authenticated principals. A general internal foothold can't touch customer data.

controls.label: Continuous attack-surface discovery + alerting
controls.detail: Run discovery on a schedule and alert on new or changed assets. It doesn't sever the chain, but it surfaces the forgotten host and the open bucket as findings — days before an attacker chains them.
